m.dhyana.1: Oṃ. O Mother Bhagavad Gītā, taught to Pārtha by Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, woven by the ancient sage Vyāsa into the midst of the Mahābhārata, showering the nectar of non-duality, the blessed one of eighteen adhyāyas, the foe of worldly bondage — on you I meditate again and again.
m.dhyana.2: Salutations to you, O Vyāsa of vast intellect, with eyes long as the petals of a full-blown lotus, by whom the lamp of knowledge, filled with the oil of the Mahābhārata, was lit.
m.dhyana.3: Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the wish-fulfilling pārijāta tree for those who take refuge in him, who holds the goad and the cane in one hand, who shows the gesture of knowledge, and who milks the nectar of the Gītā.
m.dhyana.4: All the Upaniṣads are the cows; the one who milks them is Kṛṣṇa, the joy of the cowherds; Pārtha is the calf; the wise are those who drink; and the milk is the great nectar of the Gītā.
m.dhyana.5: I bow to Kṛṣṇa, the teacher of the world, the divine son of Vasudeva, the crusher of Kaṃsa and Cāṇūra, the supreme joy of Devakī.
m.dhyana.6: The river of battle, whose banks were Bhīṣma and Droṇa, whose water was Jayadratha, whose blue lotus was Gāndhārī, whose crocodile was Śalya, whose current was Kṛpa, whose shore surged with Karṇa, whose fearsome sea-monsters were Aśvatthāmā and Vikarṇa, and whose whirlpool was Duryodhana — that river the Pāṇḍavas indeed crossed, for Keśava was their boatman.
m.dhyana.7: May the spotless lotus of the Mahābhārata, born of the words of Parāśara's son, rich with the fragrance of the Gītā's meaning, its filaments the many tales, opened by the telling of Hari's story, drunk with joy again and again, day after day, by the good of the world as by bees, the destroyer of the impurity of the Kali age, be for our highest good.
m.dhyana.8: I bow to that Mādhava, the supreme bliss, whose grace makes the mute eloquent and the lame cross mountains.
m.dhyana.9: Salutations to that God whom Brahmā, Varuṇa, Indra, Rudra and the Maruts praise with divine hymns; whom the singers of the Sāma sing with the Vedas, their limbs, their pada and krama recitations, and the Upaniṣads; whom yogīs see with minds fixed in meditation and absorbed in him; and whose end neither the hosts of the gods nor of the asuras know.
m.1.1: Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: On the field of dharma, on the field of the Kurus, gathered together and eager to fight, what did my sons and the sons of Pāṇḍu do, O Sañjaya?
m.1.2: Sañjaya said: But then, seeing the army of the Pāṇḍavas arrayed for battle, King Duryodhana approached his teacher and spoke these words.
m.1.3: Behold, O teacher, this great army of the sons of Pāṇḍu, arrayed by the son of Drupada, your wise disciple.
m.1.4: Here are heroes, great archers, equal in battle to Bhīma and Arjuna: Yuyudhāna, Virāṭa, and Drupada, the great chariot-warrior;
m.1.5: Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna, and the valiant king of Kāśī; Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Śaibya, a bull among men;
m.1.6: The bold Yudhāmanyu and the valiant Uttamaujas, Subhadrā's son and Draupadī's sons — all of them indeed great chariot-warriors.
m.1.7: But know also, O best of the twice-born, those who are foremost among us, who lead my army; I name them to you for your information.
m.1.8: Your honour, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, and Kṛpa, victorious in battle; Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, and likewise the son of Somadatta;
m.1.9: And many other heroes who have given up their lives for my sake, armed with various weapons, all skilled in warfare.
m.1.10: That army of ours, guarded by Bhīṣma, is insufficient, whereas this army of theirs, guarded by Bhīma, is sufficient.
m.1.11: So all of you, stationed in your respective positions at every point of entry, must protect Bhīṣma above all.
m.1.12: Then, bringing joy to him (Duryodhana), the mighty grandsire, the eldest of the Kurus, roared loudly like a lion and blew his conch.
m.1.13: Then conches and kettledrums, tabors, drums and cow-horns were suddenly sounded, and that noise became tumultuous.
m.1.14: Then Mādhava and the son of Pāṇḍu, standing in a great chariot yoked with white horses, blew their divine conches.
m.1.15: Hṛṣīkeśa blew the Pāñcajanya, Dhanañjaya the Devadatta; Vṛkodara, of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Pauṇḍra.
m.1.16: King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, blew the Anantavijaya; Nakula and Sahadeva the Sughoṣa and the Maṇipuṣpaka.
m.1.17: And the king of Kāśī, the supreme archer, and Śikhaṇḍin, the great chariot-warrior, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Virāṭa, and the unconquered Sātyaki;
m.1.18: Drupada and the sons of Draupadī, O lord of the earth, and the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā — all of them on every side blew their conches, each his own.
m.1.19: That tumultuous uproar, resounding through sky and earth, tore apart the hearts of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
m.1.20: Then, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra drawn up in position, as the clash of weapons was about to begin, the son of Pāṇḍu, whose banner bore the ape, raised his bow,
m.1.21: — then spoke these words to Hṛṣīkeśa, O lord of the earth. Arjuna said: O Acyuta, station my chariot between the two armies,
m.1.22: so that I may observe these who stand here eager to fight, and see with whom I must fight in this undertaking of battle.
m.1.23: I wish to see those who are about to fight, who have gathered here wishing to do in battle what pleases the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
m.1.24: Sañjaya said: Thus addressed by Guḍākeśa, O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa stationed the finest of chariots between the two armies,
m.1.25: in front of Bhīṣma and Droṇa and all the rulers of the earth, and said: O Pārtha, behold these Kurus assembled together.
m.1.26: There Pārtha saw, standing in both armies, fathers and grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and friends as well,
m.1.27: fathers-in-law and well-wishers too, in both the armies. Seeing all those kinsmen arrayed, he, the son of Kuntī,
m.1.28: overcome with deep compassion, sinking in despair, spoke this. Arjuna said: Seeing these my own people, O Kṛṣṇa, assembled and eager to fight,
m.1.29: my limbs give way and my mouth dries up; a trembling arises in my body, and my hair stands on end.
m.1.30: Gāṇḍīva slips from my hand and all my skin is burning; I cannot stand steady, and my mind seems to whirl.
m.1.31: And I see adverse omens, O Keśava, and I foresee no good in killing my own people in battle.
m.1.32: I do not desire victory, O Kṛṣṇa, nor kingdom, nor pleasures. Of what use to us is a kingdom, O Govinda, or enjoyments, or even life?
m.1.33: Those for whose sake we desired kingdom, enjoyments and pleasures—they stand here in battle, having staked their lives and wealth:
m.1.34: teachers, fathers, sons, and likewise grandfathers, uncles on the mother's side, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other kinsmen besides.
m.1.35: These I do not wish to kill, even if they kill me, O Madhusūdana—not even for the sovereignty of the three worlds, how much less for the sake of the earth?
m.1.36: Having slain the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, what joy would be ours, O Janārdana? Sin alone would cling to us for killing these aggressors.
m.1.37: Therefore we ought not to kill the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, our own kinsmen. For how could we be happy after killing our own people, O Mādhava?
m.1.38: Even though these, their minds overpowered by greed, do not see the evil caused by destroying a family, and the sin in betraying friends,
m.1.39: why should we not know to turn away from this sin—we who clearly see the evil caused by destroying a family, O Janārdana?
m.1.40: When a family is destroyed, its ancient family dharmas perish; when dharma is lost, adharma overcomes the whole family.
m.1.41: When adharma prevails, O Kṛṣṇa, the women of the family become corrupted; when women are corrupted, O Vārṣṇeya, intermixture of varṇas arises.
m.1.42: This intermixture leads to hell itself, both for the family-destroyers and for the family; for their ancestors fall, deprived of the rites of piṇḍa and water offerings.
m.1.43: By these misdeeds of the family-destroyers, which cause intermixture of varṇas, the dharmas of the community and the everlasting family dharmas are uprooted.
m.1.44: For men whose family dharmas are destroyed, O Janārdana, dwelling in hell is certain—so we have heard.
m.1.45: Alas! What a great sin we have resolved to commit, that out of greed for the pleasures of kingship we are ready to kill our own people!
m.1.46: If the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, weapons in hand, should kill me in battle while I am unresisting and unarmed, that would be better for me.
m.1.47: Sañjaya said: Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna sat down on the seat of the chariot, casting aside his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed with grief.
m.1.iti: Oṃ Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the first adhyāya, named Arjunaviṣādayoga, the yoga of Arjuna’s despondency.
m.2.1: Sañjaya said: To him, who was thus overcome by pity, whose eyes were troubled and filled with tears, and who was sinking in despair, Madhusūdana spoke these words.
m.2.2: The Lord said: From where has this dejection come upon you at this critical hour, O Arjuna? It is not practised by noble men, it does not lead to heaven, and it brings disgrace.
m.2.3: Do not yield to unmanliness, O Pārtha; it does not befit you. Casting off this petty weakness of heart, stand up, O scorcher of foes.
m.2.4: Arjuna said: How shall I, O Madhusūdana, fight back in battle with arrows against Bhīṣma and Droṇa, who are both worthy of worship, O slayer of enemies?
m.2.5: Better indeed, in this world, to live even on alms than to slay these noble-souled teachers. For if I slay these teachers, though they are desirous of gain, I should enjoy here itself pleasures smeared with blood.
m.2.6: Nor do we know which is better for us—whether we should conquer them or they should conquer us. The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having slain whom we would not even wish to live, stand arrayed before us.
m.2.7: My nature is overcome by the fault of faint-hearted pity, and my mind is bewildered about dharma; I ask you: tell me for certain what is better. I am your disciple; instruct me, who have taken refuge in you.
m.2.8: For I do not see what could remove this grief of mine that dries up my senses, even if I were to gain on earth an unrivalled, prosperous kingdom, or even lordship over the gods.
m.2.9: Sañjaya said: Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, Guḍākeśa (Arjuna), O scorcher of foes, said to Govinda, “I will not fight,” and fell silent.
m.2.10: O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa, as if smiling, spoke these words to him who was despairing between the two armies.
m.2.11: The Lord said: You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for, and yet you speak words of wisdom. The wise do not grieve for those whose life has departed nor for those whose life has not departed.
m.2.12: Never indeed was there a time when I did not exist, or you, or these rulers of men; nor shall any of us ever cease to be hereafter.
m.2.13: Just as the embodied one passes in this body through childhood, youth and old age, so too it attains another body; the steadfast one is not bewildered by this.
m.2.14: But the contacts of the senses with their objects, O son of Kuntī, give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain; they arrive and depart and are impermanent. Endure them, O Bhārata.
m.2.15: The steadfast person whom these do not disturb, O best of men, who remains the same in pain and pleasure—he is fit for immortality.
m.2.16: The unreal has no being, and the real has no non-being. The final truth about both of these has been seen by the seers of reality.
m.2.17: Know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded. No one can bring about the destruction of this imperishable one.
m.2.18: These bodies of the eternal, indestructible, immeasurable embodied one are said to have an end. Therefore fight, O Bhārata.
m.2.19: He who thinks this one is a slayer, and he who thinks this one is slain—both do not understand. This one neither slays nor is slain.
m.2.20: It is never born, nor does it ever die; nor, having come into being, will it again cease to be. Unborn, eternal, everlasting and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.
m.2.21: He who knows this one to be indestructible, eternal, unborn and imperishable—how, O Pārtha, can that person slay anyone, or cause anyone to be slain?
m.2.22: Just as a man casts off worn-out clothes and takes on other, new ones, so the embodied one casts off worn-out bodies and enters other, new ones.
m.2.23: Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it, waters do not wet it, and wind does not dry it.
m.2.24: It cannot be cut, it cannot be burnt, it cannot be wetted nor dried. It is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable and everlasting.
m.2.25: It is said to be unmanifest, unthinkable and unchangeable. Therefore, knowing it to be so, you should not grieve.
m.2.26: And even if you think of this Self as constantly being born and constantly dying, even then, O mighty-armed one, you should not grieve like this.
m.2.27: For death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died. Therefore, over a matter that cannot be avoided, you should not grieve.
m.2.28: Beings are unmanifest in their beginning, manifest in their middle, O Bhārata, and unmanifest again in their end. What is there to lament in this?
m.2.29: One sees this Self as a wonder; another likewise speaks of it as a wonder; another hears of it as a wonder; and even having heard, no one truly knows it.
m.2.30: This embodied one dwelling in the body of every being is ever unslayable, O Bhārata. Therefore you should not grieve for any beings.
m.2.31: Moreover, considering your own duty, you should not waver; for nothing is better for a kṣatriya than a righteous war.
m.2.32: Fortunate are the kṣatriyas, O Pārtha, who obtain such a war, come of its own accord as an open door to heaven.
m.2.33: But if you do not fight this righteous battle, then, abandoning your own duty and honour, you will incur sin.
m.2.34: People will also speak of your undying disgrace; and for one who has been honoured, disgrace is worse than death.
m.2.35: The great chariot-warriors will think you withdrew from battle out of fear; and among those by whom you were highly esteemed, you will fall into lightness.
m.2.36: Your enemies will say many unspeakable things, deriding your ability. What could be more painful than that?
m.2.37: Either, slain, you will attain heaven, or, victorious, you will enjoy the earth. Therefore arise, O Kaunteya, resolved to fight.
m.2.38: Treating alike pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat, then engage in battle; thus you will not incur sin.
m.2.39: This understanding has been declared to you according to Sāṅkhya; now hear it according to Yoga, joined with which understanding, O Pārtha, you will cast off the bondage of action.
m.2.40: Here no effort is lost and no adverse result arises. Even a little of this dharma protects from great fear.
m.2.41: Here, O joy of the Kurus, the resolute understanding is single; but the understandings of the irresolute are many-branched and endless.
m.2.42: This flowery speech, O Pārtha, which the unwise proclaim, delighting in the words of the Veda and saying “there is nothing else”—
m.2.43: —they whose nature is desire, intent on heaven, proclaim speech that yields birth as the fruit of action and abounds in special rites aimed at enjoyment and power.
m.2.44: For those attached to enjoyment and power, whose minds are carried away by that speech, a resolute understanding is not established in samādhi.
m.2.45: The Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain; be free of the three guṇas, O Arjuna—free of the pairs of opposites, ever established in sattva, free of concern for acquiring and keeping, and possessed of the Self.
m.2.46: As much use as there is in a small well when there is water flooding on all sides, so much use is there in all the Vedas for a brāhmaṇa who truly knows.
m.2.47: Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction.
m.2.48: Established in yoga, perform actions, abandoning attachment, O Dhanañjaya, being even-minded in success and failure. Evenness is called yoga.
m.2.49: Action is far inferior to the yoga of understanding, O Dhanañjaya. Seek refuge in understanding; pitiable are those whose motive is the fruit.
m.2.50: One joined with understanding casts off here both good and evil deeds. Therefore devote yourself to yoga; yoga is skill in actions.
m.2.51: For the wise, joined with this understanding, give up the fruit born of action. Freed from the bondage of birth, they go to the state that is free from all ill.
m.2.52: When your understanding crosses beyond the mire of delusion, then you will become indifferent to what is yet to be heard and what has been heard.
m.2.53: When your understanding, now bewildered by conflicting scriptural teachings, stands unwavering and steady in samādhi, then you will attain yoga.
m.2.54: Arjuna said: What is the description of one whose wisdom is steady, who is established in samādhi, O Keśava? How would one of steady mind speak? How would he sit? How would he move?
m.2.55: The Lord said: When one gives up all the desires that have entered the mind, O Pārtha, content in the self by the self alone, then he is called one of steady wisdom.
m.2.56: He whose mind is not shaken in sorrows, who has no craving for pleasures, from whom attachment, fear and anger have departed — he is called a sage of steady mind.
m.2.57: He who is without attachment everywhere, who, meeting with this or that, pleasant or unpleasant, neither rejoices nor hates — his wisdom is firmly established.
m.2.58: And when he withdraws his senses from the objects of the senses on every side, as a tortoise draws in its limbs, his wisdom is firmly established.
m.2.59: The objects fall away from the embodied one who abstains from them, except the taste for them; even the taste of this one falls away on seeing the Supreme.
m.2.60: For, O Kaunteya, the turbulent senses forcibly carry away the mind even of a discerning man who is striving.
m.2.61: Having restrained them all, he should sit disciplined, intent on me; for he whose senses are under control — his wisdom is firmly established.
m.2.62: In a man who dwells on sense objects, attachment to them arises; from attachment desire is born; from desire anger arises.
m.2.63: From anger comes delusion; from delusion, confusion of memory; from the loss of memory, the ruin of understanding; from the ruin of understanding, one perishes.
m.2.64: But one whose self is disciplined, who moves among the objects of the senses with senses under his own control and free from attraction and aversion, attains serenity.
m.2.65: In serenity, the end of all his sorrows comes about; for the understanding of one whose mind is serene soon becomes firmly settled.
m.2.66: For the undisciplined there is no understanding, nor does the undisciplined have contemplation; for one without contemplation there is no peace; for one without peace, whence happiness?
m.2.67: For when the mind follows the roaming senses, it carries away his wisdom, as the wind carries away a boat on the water.
m.2.68: Therefore, O mighty-armed one, he whose senses are wholly withdrawn from the objects of the senses — his wisdom is firmly established.
m.2.69: What is night for all beings, in that the self-restrained one is awake; that in which beings are awake is night for the sage who sees.
m.2.70: As the waters enter the ocean, which is ever being filled yet remains unmoved in its bed, so he whom all desires enter attains peace — not the one who desires desires.
m.2.71: The man who, having given up all desires, moves about free from craving, without the sense of “mine”, without ego — he attains peace.
m.2.72: This is the Brahmic state, O Pārtha; having attained it, one is not deluded. Abiding in it even at the time of death, one reaches nirvāṇa in Brahman.
m.2.iti: Oṃ Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the second adhyāya, named Sāṅkhyayoga, the yoga of Sāṅkhya.
m.3.1: Arjuna said: If you hold that understanding is superior to action, O Janārdana, then why do you urge me into this dreadful action, O Keśava?
m.3.2: With seemingly mixed-up words you appear to confuse my understanding. So tell me decisively the one thing by which I may attain the highest good.
m.3.3: The Lord said: In this world a twofold path was declared by me of old, O sinless one: for the Sāṅkhyas, through the discipline of knowledge; for the yogins, through the discipline of action.
m.3.4: Not by abstaining from actions does a person attain freedom from action, nor by mere renunciation does he reach perfection.
m.3.5: For no one can ever remain even for a moment without doing action; everyone is made to act, helplessly, by the guṇas born of prakṛti.
m.3.6: He who restrains the organs of action but sits dwelling in mind on the sense objects, deluded in himself, is called a hypocrite.
m.3.7: But he who, controlling the senses by the mind, O Arjuna, undertakes the yoga of action with the organs of action, unattached, he excels.
m.3.8: Do your prescribed action, for action is better than inaction; even the maintenance of your body would not be possible without action.
m.3.9: This world is bound by action, except for action done for the sake of sacrifice. For that purpose, O son of Kuntī, perform action free from attachment.
m.3.10: Having created beings together with sacrifice, Prajāpati said of old: “By this you shall multiply; let this be your cow that yields desired wishes.”
m.3.11: “Nourish the gods with this, and let those gods nourish you; nourishing one another, you will attain the highest good.”
m.3.12: “Nourished by sacrifice, the gods will give you the enjoyments you desire.” he who enjoys what they have given without offering to them is surely a thief.
m.3.13: The good who eat the remnants of sacrifice are freed from all sins; but the wicked who cook for their own sake eat sin.
m.3.14: Beings arise from food; food comes from rain; rain arises from sacrifice; sacrifice is born of action.
m.3.15: Know that action arises from Brahman (the Veda), and Brahman arises from the Imperishable. Therefore the all-pervading Brahman is ever established in sacrifice.
m.3.16: He who here does not follow the wheel thus set in motion, living in sin and delighting in the senses, lives in vain, O Pārtha.
m.3.17: But the man who delights in the Self alone, is satisfied in the Self, and is content in the Self alone—for him there is nothing that must be done.
m.3.18: For him there is no purpose at all here in what is done, nor in what is not done; nor does he depend on any being for any purpose.
m.3.19: Therefore, always unattached, perform well the action that must be done; for by performing action without attachment a person attains the Supreme.
m.3.20: Indeed, it was through action alone that Janaka and others attained perfection. Even having regard for the welfare of the world, you ought to act.
m.3.21: Whatever the best person does, that alone other people do; whatever standard he sets, the world follows that.
m.3.22: For me, O Pārtha, there is nothing at all to be done in the three worlds, nor anything unattained to be attained; yet I continue in action.
m.3.23: For if I were ever not to engage in action untiringly, men would follow my path in every way, O Pārtha.
m.3.24: These worlds would perish if I did not perform action; I would be the cause of confusion of the social order and would destroy these beings.
m.3.25: As the unwise act attached to action, O Bhārata, so should the wise act unattached, wishing to maintain the order of the world.
m.3.26: The wise man should not create a split in the understanding of the ignorant who are attached to action; rather, himself acting steadfastly in yoga, he should engage them in all actions.
m.3.27: Actions are in every way being performed by the guṇas of prakṛti; yet one whose self is deluded by ego thinks, “I am the doer.”
m.3.28: But one who knows the truth about the divisions of guṇas and actions, O mighty-armed one, thinking “the guṇas move among the guṇas,” does not become attached.
m.3.29: Those deluded by the guṇas of prakṛti become attached to the workings of the guṇas; the knower of the whole should not unsettle those dull ones of partial knowledge.
m.3.30: Surrendering all actions to me with a mind fixed on the Self, free from desire and from the sense of “mine,” fight, with your fever of anguish gone.
m.3.31: Those men who constantly follow this teaching of mine, full of faith and not finding fault, they too are freed from the bondage of actions.
m.3.32: But those who, finding fault with it, do not follow this teaching of mine — know them, deluded in all knowledge and devoid of discernment, to be lost.
m.3.33: Even a man of knowledge acts in accordance with his own nature; beings follow their nature — what will repression accomplish?
m.3.34: Attraction and aversion are set in each sense towards its object; one should not come under their sway, for they are his adversaries.
m.3.35: Better is one's own dharma, though imperfect, than another's dharma well performed. Death in one's own dharma is better; another's dharma is fraught with danger.
m.3.36: Arjuna said: Then, impelled by what does a man commit sin, even against his will, O Vārṣṇeya, as if forced to it?
m.3.37: The Lord said: It is desire, it is anger, born of the guṇa of rajas, all-devouring, greatly sinful; know this to be the enemy here.
m.3.38: As fire is covered by smoke, and a mirror by dust, as an embryo is enveloped by the womb, so is this knowledge covered by that desire.
m.3.39: Knowledge is covered, O Kaunteya, by this enemy of the wise that never ceases, which takes the form of desire, an insatiable fire.
m.3.40: The senses, the mind and the intellect are said to be its seat; through these it deludes the embodied one, veiling his knowledge.
m.3.41: Therefore, O best of the Bharatas, first restraining the senses, slay this sinful thing, the destroyer of knowledge and realisation.
m.3.42: The senses, they say, are superior to the body; higher than the senses is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect; but what is beyond the intellect is he the Self.
m.3.43: Thus knowing that which is beyond the intellect, steadying the self by the Self, slay, O mighty-armed one, the enemy in the form of desire, so hard to overcome.
m.3.iti: Oṃ Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the third adhyāya, named Karmayoga, the yoga of action.
m.4.1: The Lord said: I declared this imperishable yoga to Vivasvān; Vivasvān told it to Manu, and Manu spoke it to Ikṣvāku.
m.4.2: Thus received through succession, the royal sages knew it. But through long time, O scorcher of foes, that yoga was lost here in the world.
m.4.3: That same ancient yoga has been declared by me to you today, since you are my devotee and friend; for this is the supreme secret.
m.4.4: Arjuna said: Your birth is later; the birth of Vivasvān is earlier. How am I to understand that you declared it in the beginning?
m.4.5: The Lord said: Many births of mine have passed, and of yours too, O Arjuna. I know them all; you do not know them, O scorcher of foes.
m.4.6: Though I am unborn, of imperishable nature, and though I am the lord of beings, governing my own prakṛti, I come into being by my own māyā.
m.4.7: Whenever there is a decline of dharma, O Bhārata, and a rise of adharma, then I send forth myself.
m.4.8: To protect the good, to destroy evildoers, and to establish dharma firmly, I come into being age after age.
m.4.9: He who thus truly knows my divine birth and action, on leaving the body, does not go to rebirth; he comes to me, O Arjuna.
m.4.10: Free from attachment, fear and anger, absorbed in me, taking refuge in me, many, purified by the austerity of knowledge, have attained my being.
m.4.11: In whatever way people approach me, in that very way I respond to them. Human beings follow my path in every way, O Pārtha.
m.4.12: Desiring success in their actions, people here worship the deities; for in the human world success born of action comes quickly.
m.4.13: The fourfold order was created by me according to the division of qualities (guṇa) and actions. Though I am its maker, know me as the non-doer, the imperishable.
m.4.14: Actions do not taint me, nor have I any longing for the fruit of action. He who knows me thus is not bound by actions.
m.4.15: Knowing thus, action was performed even by the ancient seekers of liberation. Therefore you too should perform action, as was done by the ancients in former times.
m.4.16: What is action, what is inaction — even the wise are bewildered here. I shall explain to you that action, knowing which you will be freed from the inauspicious.
m.4.17: For one must understand the nature of action, one must understand that of wrong action, and one must understand that of inaction; deep is the way of action.
m.4.18: He who sees inaction in action and action in inaction is wise among men; he is a yogī, a performer of all action.
m.4.19: He whose every undertaking is free from desire and its intention, whose actions are burnt by the fire of knowledge — him the wise call a paṇḍita.
m.4.20: Having given up attachment to the fruit of action, ever content, dependent on nothing, though fully engaged in action, he does nothing at all.
m.4.21: Without expectation, with mind and self restrained, having given up all possessions, doing merely bodily action, he incurs no sin.
m.4.22: Content with what comes by chance, beyond the pairs of opposites, free from envy, even-minded in success and failure, he is not bound even when he acts.
m.4.23: For one whose attachment is gone, who is free, whose mind is established in knowledge, and who acts for the sake of sacrifice, action dissolves entirely.
m.4.24: The act of offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, offered by Brahman into the fire of Brahman; Brahman alone is to be reached by him who is absorbed in Brahman as action.
m.4.25: Some yogīs perform sacrifice to the gods alone; others offer sacrifice by sacrifice itself into the fire of Brahman.
m.4.26: Some offer the senses, hearing and the rest, into the fires of restraint; others offer the sense-objects, sound and the rest, into the fires of the senses.
m.4.27: Others offer all the actions of the senses and the actions of the life-breath into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint, kindled by knowledge.
m.4.28: Others likewise offer material possessions as sacrifice, austerity as sacrifice, yoga as sacrifice; and ascetics of rigorous vows offer study of scripture and knowledge as sacrifice.
m.4.29: Likewise others, devoted to breath-control, having restrained the movements of the in-breath and out-breath, offer the prāṇa into the apāna and the apāna into the prāṇa.
m.4.30: Others, regulating their food, offer the life-breaths into the life-breaths. All these are knowers of sacrifice, their impurities destroyed by sacrifice.
m.4.31: Eating the nectar that remains from sacrifice, they go to the eternal Brahman. This world is not for one who does not sacrifice; how then the other, O best of the Kurus?
m.4.32: Thus sacrifices of many kinds are spread out at the mouth of Brahman (the Veda). Know them all to be born of action; knowing thus, you will be liberated.
m.4.33: Better than sacrifice made of material things is the sacrifice of knowledge, O scorcher of foes. All action without exception, O Pārtha, culminates in knowledge.
m.4.34: Know that by prostration, by thorough inquiry and by service. The wise, who have seen the truth, will teach you knowledge.
m.4.35: Knowing which, you will not again fall into delusion like this, O Pāṇḍava; by which you will see all beings without exception in the Self, and then in me.
m.4.36: Even if you are the worst sinner among all sinners, you will cross over all wrongdoing by the raft of knowledge alone.
m.4.37: As a blazing fire turns firewood to ashes, O Arjuna, so the fire of knowledge turns all actions to ashes.
m.4.38: Indeed, there is nothing here as purifying as knowledge. One perfected in yoga finds it oneself within the Self in due time.
m.4.39: The one who has faith, who is devoted to it and has controlled the senses, attains knowledge; having attained knowledge, he quickly reaches supreme peace.
m.4.40: The ignorant, the faithless and the doubting self perishes. For the doubting self there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness.
m.4.41: Actions do not bind one who has renounced actions through yoga, whose doubts are cut asunder by knowledge, and who is possessed of the Self, O Dhanañjaya.
m.4.42: Therefore, having cut with the sword of knowledge this doubt of your own, born of ignorance and lodged in the heart, take refuge in yoga; arise, O Bhārata!
m.4.iti: Oṃ Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the fourth adhyāya, named Jñānakarmasaṃnyāsayoga, the yoga of knowledge and the renunciation of action.
m.5.1: Arjuna said: O Kṛṣṇa, you praise the renunciation of actions, and then again you praise yoga. Tell me with certainty that one of these two which is the better.
m.5.2: The Lord said: Renunciation and the yoga of action both lead to the highest good; but of the two, the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action.
m.5.3: He should be known as a constant renunciant who neither hates nor craves; for, free from the pairs of opposites, O mighty-armed one, he is easily released from bondage.
m.5.4: The childish, not the wise, speak of Sāṅkhya and Yoga as different. One who is properly established in even one obtains the fruit of both.
m.5.5: The state that is reached by the Sāṅkhyas is attained by the Yogins too. He who sees Sāṅkhya and Yoga as one truly sees.
m.5.6: But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is hard to attain without yoga; the sage disciplined in yoga reaches Brahman before long.
m.5.7: Disciplined in yoga, pure in self, self-controlled, with senses conquered, whose self has become the self of all beings—he is not tainted even while acting.
m.5.8: “I do nothing at all”—so should the disciplined knower of truth think, while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing,
m.5.9: speaking, releasing, grasping, opening and closing the eyes—holding firmly that only the senses are engaged with the objects of the senses.
m.5.10: He who acts having placed his actions in Brahman, abandoning attachment, is not tainted by sin, as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
m.5.11: With the body, with the mind, with the intellect, even with the senses alone, yogins perform action, abandoning attachment, for the purification of the self.
m.5.12: The disciplined one, abandoning the fruit of action, attains lasting peace; the undisciplined one, attached to the fruit through the impulse of desire, is bound.
m.5.13: Renouncing all actions with the mind, the self-controlled embodied one dwells happily in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing anything to act.
m.5.14: The Lord does not create agency, nor actions for the world, nor the connection of action with its fruit; it is one's own nature that proceeds.
m.5.15: The all-pervading one takes on no one's sin, nor indeed anyone's good deed. Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; by that, beings are deluded.
m.5.16: But for those in whom that ignorance of the self has been destroyed by knowledge, their knowledge, like the sun, illumines that Supreme.
m.5.17: With their intellect fixed on That, their self in That, devoted to That, holding That as the supreme goal, their impurities shaken off by knowledge, they go to the state from which there is no return.
m.5.18: The wise see with an equal eye a brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and humility, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcaste.
m.5.19: Even here in this life, creation is conquered by those whose mind is established in equality; for Brahman is flawless and equal, therefore they are established in Brahman.
m.5.20: One should not rejoice on obtaining the pleasant, nor be troubled on obtaining the unpleasant; firm of intellect, undeluded, the knower of Brahman is established in Brahman.
m.5.21: One whose self is unattached to external contacts finds the happiness that is in the self; he, his self joined to Brahman through yoga, enjoys imperishable happiness.
m.5.22: For the enjoyments born of contact are indeed sources of sorrow; they have a beginning and an end, O son of Kuntī. The wise one does not delight in them.
m.5.23: He who is able, even here, before release from the body, to withstand the surge arising from desire and anger—he is disciplined, he is a happy man.
m.5.24: He whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and likewise whose light is within—that yogin, having become Brahman, attains the nirvāṇa of Brahman.
m.5.25: The seers whose impurities are destroyed, whose doubts are cut away, who are self-controlled and delight in the welfare of all beings, attain the nirvāṇa of Brahman.
m.5.26: For the ascetics who are free from desire and anger, whose minds are controlled, and who have known the Self, the bliss of Brahman (brahma-nirvāṇa) exists on all sides both here and hereafter.
m.5.27: Having shut out external contacts, and fixing the gaze between the eyebrows, having made even the outgoing and incoming breaths that move within the nostrils—
m.5.28: —the sage whose senses, mind and intellect are controlled, who is intent on liberation, and from whom desire, fear and anger have departed—he is indeed ever liberated.
m.5.29: Knowing me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great Lord of all the worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace.
m.5.iti: Oṃ Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the fifth adhyāya, named Saṃnyāsayoga, the yoga of renunciation.
m.6.1: The Lord said: He who does the work that ought to be done, without depending on the fruit of action, is a renunciant and a yogī; not the one who has merely given up the sacred fires, nor the one who has given up action.
m.6.2: What they call renunciation, know that to be yoga, O Pāṇḍava; for no one becomes a yogī who has not renounced selfish intention.
m.6.3: For the sage who wishes to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means; for that same one, once he has ascended to yoga, calm is said to be the means.
m.6.4: When one is attached neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions, having renounced all intentions, then he is said to have ascended to yoga.
m.6.5: One should lift up oneself by oneself; one should not let oneself sink down. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.
m.6.6: The self is the friend of the self for him by whom the self has been conquered by the self; but for one who has not conquered himself, the self itself would act with hostility, like an enemy.
m.6.7: For one who has conquered himself and is deeply at peace, the supreme Self is steadily collected, in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and likewise in honour and dishonour.
m.6.8: The yogī whose self is satisfied with knowledge and realisation, who is unshakable, who has conquered the senses, for whom a clod, a stone and gold are alike, is called “yoked” in yoga.
m.6.9: One who has an equal mind towards well-wishers, friends, foes, the indifferent, the neutral, the hateful and kinsmen, and towards the virtuous and the sinful alike, excels.
m.6.10: The yogī should constantly engage himself in yoga, staying in a secluded place, alone, with mind and body controlled, free from desires and without possessions.
m.6.11: Having set up for himself, in a clean place, a firm seat, neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, deerskin and kuśa grass, one after another —
m.6.12: — sitting there on that seat, making the mind one-pointed, with the activities of mind and senses controlled, he should practise yoga to purify the self.
m.6.13: Holding body, head and neck erect and motionless, steady, gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking around in any direction —
m.6.14: — serene in mind, rid of fear, firm in the vow of celibacy, restraining the mind, with thought fixed on me, he should sit yoked in yoga, holding me as the supreme goal.
m.6.15: Thus always engaging himself, the yogī of disciplined mind attains peace — the supreme nirvāṇa — that abides in me.
m.6.16: Yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all; nor for one given to too much sleep, nor indeed for one who stays awake too much, O Arjuna.
m.6.17: For one who is moderate in food and recreation, moderate in exertion in actions, and moderate in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.
m.6.18: When the well-restrained mind rests in the Self alone, free from craving for all desires, then one is said to be “yoked”.
m.6.19: “As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker” — that is the simile remembered for the yogī of controlled mind who practises the yoga of the Self.
m.6.20: Where the mind, restrained by the practice of yoga, comes to rest, and where, seeing the Self by the self, one is content in the Self —
m.6.21: — where he knows that infinite happiness which is grasped by the intellect and lies beyond the senses, and, established there, he never moves away from the truth —
m.6.22: — having gained which, he does not consider any other gain greater than it, and established in which, he is not shaken even by heavy sorrow —
m.6.23: — let one know that disconnection from union with sorrow to be what is called yoga. This yoga should be practised with determination and with an undespairing mind.
m.6.24: Abandoning completely all desires born of intention, and restraining the whole troop of senses on every side by the mind alone,
m.6.25: one should gradually come to rest, through the intellect held firm by steadfastness; having made the mind abide in the Self, one should think of nothing at all.
m.6.26: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders off, from there one should draw it back and bring it under control in the Self alone.
m.6.27: For supreme happiness comes to this yogī whose mind is fully calm, whose passion (rajas) is stilled, who has become one with Brahman and is free from taint.
m.6.28: Thus ever engaging himself in yoga, the yogī, freed from taint, easily attains the boundless happiness of contact with Brahman.
m.6.29: One whose self is joined in yoga, seeing with an equal eye everywhere, sees the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self.
m.6.30: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me — to him I am never lost, and he is never lost to me.
m.6.31: The yogī who, established in oneness, worships me as abiding in all beings, abides in me, however he may be living.
m.6.32: O Arjuna, one who, by comparison with himself, sees equally everywhere, whether in pleasure or in pain — that yogī is considered the highest.
m.6.33: Arjuna said: This yoga of equanimity that you have taught, O Madhusūdana — because of the mind's restlessness, I do not see its steady foundation.
m.6.34: For the mind is restless, O Kṛṣṇa, turbulent, powerful and obstinate; I think restraining it is as very hard as restraining the wind.
m.6.35: The Lord said: Without doubt, O mighty-armed one, the mind is hard to restrain and restless; but, O son of Kuntī, it is held in check by practice and by dispassion.
m.6.36: Yoga is hard to attain for one whose self is unrestrained — this is my view; but by one whose self is controlled and who strives, it can be attained through the right means.
m.6.37: Arjuna said: One who is endowed with faith but lacks self-control, whose mind has strayed from yoga — not having attained perfection in yoga, what end does he reach, O Kṛṣṇa?
m.6.38: Fallen from both, without support, O mighty-armed one, bewildered on the path of Brahman, does he not perish like a scattered cloud?
m.6.39: O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to dispel this doubt of mine completely; for none other than you can be found to dispel this doubt.
m.6.40: The Lord said: O Pārtha, neither here nor hereafter is there destruction for him; for no one who does good, my dear, ever comes to an evil end.
m.6.41: Having reached the worlds of the righteous and dwelt there for countless years, one who has fallen from yoga is born in the home of the pure and prosperous.
m.6.42: Or else he is born in the very family of wise yogīs; but such a birth as this is very hard to obtain in the world.
m.6.43: There he regains that union with wisdom from his former body, and from there he strives again for perfection, O joy of the Kurus.
m.6.44: By that very former practice he is carried onward, even without his will; even one who merely wishes to know yoga goes beyond the Vedic word (śabda-brahman).
m.6.45: But the yogī who strives with diligence, cleansed of sins, perfected through many births, then reaches the supreme goal.
m.6.46: The yogī is superior to ascetics, considered superior even to men of knowledge, and superior to men of ritual action; therefore, O Arjuna, be a yogī.
m.6.47: And of all yogīs, the one who, full of faith, worships me with his inner self absorbed in me — he is considered by me the most united in yoga.
m.6.iti: Oṃ Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the sixth adhyāya, named Ātmasaṃyamayoga, the yoga of self-control.
m.7.1: The Lord said: With your mind attached to me, O Pārtha, practising yoga and taking refuge in me, hear how you will know me fully and without doubt.
m.7.2: I shall teach you in full this knowledge together with realised understanding, having known which nothing else remains here to be known.
m.7.3: Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection; and even among those who strive and attain, scarcely one knows me in truth.
m.7.4: Earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and ego — thus is my nature divided eightfold.
m.7.5: This is the lower; but know, O mighty-armed, my other, higher nature, distinct from this — the life-principle by which this world is sustained.
m.7.6: Understand that all beings have these two natures as their source. I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the whole world.
m.7.7: There is nothing whatever higher than me, O Dhanañjaya. All this is strung on me like clusters of gems on a thread.
m.7.8: I am the taste in water, O Kaunteya; I am the radiance of the moon and the sun; the syllable Om in all the Vedas, sound in space, manliness in men.
m.7.9: I am the pure fragrance in the earth and the brilliance in fire; I am the life in all beings and the austerity in ascetics.
m.7.10: Know me, O Pārtha, as the everlasting seed of all beings. I am the intelligence of the intelligent, the brilliance of the brilliant.
m.7.11: I am the strength of the strong, free from desire and passion; and in beings I am desire that is not opposed to dharma, O best of the Bhāratas.
m.7.12: And whatever states are sāttvika, and those that are rājasa and tāmasa — know them to be from me alone; yet I am not in them, they are in me.
m.7.13: Deluded by these three states made of the guṇas, this whole world does not recognise me, who am beyond them and imperishable.
m.7.14: For this divine māyā of mine, made of the guṇas, is hard to cross; those who take refuge in me alone cross over this māyā.
m.7.15: Evil-doers, the deluded, the lowest of men, whose knowledge is stolen by māyā and who have resorted to a demonic disposition, do not take refuge in me.
m.7.16: Four kinds of virtuous people worship me, O Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, O best of the Bhāratas.
m.7.17: Of them the wise one, ever steadfast and of single devotion, excels; for I am exceedingly dear to the wise one, and he is dear to me.
m.7.18: All these are indeed noble, but the wise one I consider my very Self; for he, with a steadfast mind, abides in me alone as the supreme goal.
m.7.19: At the end of many births the wise one takes refuge in me, knowing “Vāsudeva is all.” Such a great soul is very rare.
m.7.20: Those whose knowledge is carried away by various desires resort to other deities, following this or that observance, constrained by their own nature.
m.7.21: Whatever form any devotee wishes to worship with faith, that very faith of his I make unwavering.
m.7.22: Endowed with that faith, he seeks to worship that deity, and from it obtains his desires — though those are in truth ordained by me alone.
m.7.23: But the fruit gained by those of small understanding is finite. Worshippers of the gods go to the gods; my devotees come to me.
m.7.24: The unintelligent think of me, the unmanifest, as having become manifest, not knowing my supreme nature, imperishable and unsurpassed.
m.7.25: Veiled by my yoga-māyā, I am not revealed to all. This deluded world does not recognise me, the unborn and imperishable.
m.7.26: I know the beings that have passed away, those that are present, and those that are yet to come, O Arjuna; but no one knows me.
m.7.27: O Bhārata, O scorcher of foes, through the delusion of the pairs of opposites arising from desire and aversion, all beings fall into bewilderment at birth.
m.7.28: But those people of virtuous deeds whose sin has come to an end, freed from the delusion of the pairs of opposites, worship me with firm resolve.
m.7.29: Those who, taking refuge in me, strive for freedom from old age and death, they know that Brahman fully, know the Self within (adhyātma), and action in its entirety.
m.7.30: Those who know me together with the adhibhūta, the adhidaiva, and the adhiyajña, they, with minds steadfast, know me even at the time of departure from the body.
m.7.iti: Oṃ Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the seventh adhyāya, named Jñānavijñānayoga, the yoga of knowledge and realised knowledge.
m.8.1: Arjuna said: What is that Brahman? What is adhyātma the inner self? What is karma, O Supreme Person? And what is declared to be adhibhūta that which pertains to beings? What is called adhidaiva that which pertains to the gods?
m.8.2: Who is adhiyajña, the one presiding over sacrifice here in this body, and how is he so, O Madhusūdana? And how are you known at the time of departure by those whose minds are controlled?
m.8.3: The Lord said: Brahman is the supreme Imperishable; its own nature as the indwelling self is called adhyātma; the creative offering that brings beings into existence is termed karma.
m.8.4: Adhibhūta is perishable existence; the Person (Puruṣa) is adhidaivata; and adhiyajña is I myself, here in the body, O best of the embodied.
m.8.5: And whoever, at the time of the end, remembering me alone, departs having left the body, attains my state; there is no doubt about this.
m.8.6: Whatever state of being one remembers when at the end one leaves the body, to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, having always been absorbed in that state.
m.8.7: Therefore at all times remember me and fight. With mind and intellect offered to me, you will surely come to me, without doubt.
m.8.8: With a mind disciplined by the yoga of practice, not straying elsewhere, constantly meditating, O Pārtha, one goes to the supreme divine Person.
m.8.9: Whoever would meditate on the Seer, the Ancient, the Ruler, subtler than the subtle, the Sustainer of all, of inconceivable form, sun-coloured, beyond darkness—
m.8.10: —at the time of departure, with an unmoving mind, joined with devotion and by the power of yoga, having fully fixed the life-breath between the eyebrows, he reaches that supreme divine Person.
m.8.11: That which the knowers of the Veda call the Imperishable, which ascetics free from passion enter, desiring which they live a life of celibacy—that goal I shall declare to you briefly.
m.8.12: Having restrained all the gates of the senses, confined the mind in the heart, placed one's life-breath in the head, and established in yogic concentration—
m.8.13: —uttering “Om”, the one-syllabled Brahman, and remembering me, whoever departs leaving the body attains the supreme goal.
m.8.14: He who, with mind on nothing else, constantly remembers me day after day—for that yogin, ever united, I am easy to reach, O Pārtha.
m.8.15: Having come to me, the great-souled, who have reached the highest perfection, do not again take birth, which is the abode of sorrow and impermanent.
m.8.16: All worlds, up to the realm of Brahmā, are subject to return, O Arjuna; but having come to me, O son of Kuntī, there is no rebirth.
m.8.17: Those people who know day and night truly know that a day of Brahmā extends to a thousand yugas, and his night ends with a thousand yugas.
m.8.18: At the coming of Brahmā's day, all manifest things come forth from the unmanifest; at the coming of night they dissolve into that very thing called the unmanifest.
m.8.19: This same multitude of beings, coming into being again and again, dissolves helplessly at the coming of night, O Pārtha, and comes forth at the coming of day.
m.8.20: But beyond that unmanifest there is another, eternal unmanifest being, which does not perish when all beings perish.
m.8.21: That unmanifest is called the Imperishable; they call it the supreme goal. Having reached it, they do not return. That is my supreme abode.
m.8.22: That supreme Person, O Pārtha, within whom all beings abide and by whom all this is pervaded, is attainable by undivided devotion.
m.8.23: Now I shall tell you, O bull of the Bharatas, the time at which yogins, departing, go to non-return and also to return.
m.8.24: Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the sun's northern course—departing then, people who know Brahman go to Brahman.
m.8.25: Smoke, night, likewise the dark fortnight, the six months of the sun's southern course—departing then, the yogin, having reached the lunar light, returns.
m.8.26: These two paths of the world, the bright and the dark, are indeed held to be eternal. By the one a person goes to non-return; by the other he returns again.
m.8.27: Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogī is deluded. Therefore at all times, O Arjuna, be steadfast in yoga.
m.8.28: Whatever fruit of merit is declared for the Vedas, for sacrifices, for austerities and for gifts — having known this, the yogī goes beyond all that and attains the supreme, primal abode.
m.8.iti: Oṃ Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the eighth adhyāya, named Akṣarabrahmayoga, the yoga of the imperishable Brahman.
m.9.1: The Lord said: But to you, who are free from envy, I shall declare this most secret knowledge, together with realised knowledge, knowing which you will be released from what is inauspicious.
m.9.2: This is the king of sciences, the king of secrets, the supreme purifier; it is directly perceived, in accord with dharma, very easy to practise, and imperishable.
m.9.3: People who have no faith in this dharma, O scorcher of foes, not attaining me, return to the path of death and worldly existence.
m.9.4: All this universe is pervaded by me in my unmanifest form. All beings abide in me, but I do not abide in them.
m.9.5: And yet beings do not abide in me — behold my divine yoga! Sustaining beings yet not abiding in beings, my Self is the source of beings.
m.9.6: Just as the mighty wind, moving everywhere, ever rests in space, so know that all beings rest in me.
m.9.7: All beings, O son of Kuntī, go into my prakṛti at the end of a kalpa; at the beginning of a kalpa I send them forth again.
m.9.8: Resting on my own prakṛti, I send forth again and again this entire multitude of beings, helpless under the sway of prakṛti.
m.9.9: And these actions do not bind me, O Dhanañjaya, for I sit as one indifferent, unattached to those actions.
m.9.10: With me as overseer, prakṛti brings forth all that moves and does not move; for this reason, O son of Kuntī, the world revolves.
m.9.11: Fools disregard me when I have taken on a human body, not knowing my higher nature as the great Lord of beings.
m.9.12: Vain in their hopes, vain in their actions, vain in their knowledge, senseless, they resort to the deluding nature of rākṣasas and asuras.
m.9.13: But the great-souled, O Pārtha, resorting to the divine nature, worship me with undistracted mind, knowing me as the imperishable origin of beings.
m.9.14: Always glorifying me and striving, firm in their vows, and bowing to me with devotion, ever united with me, they worship me.
m.9.15: Others, too, offering the sacrifice of knowledge, worship me, whose face is everywhere, as one, as distinct, and in many ways.
m.9.16: I am the ritual, I am the sacrifice, I am the offering to the ancestors, I am the healing herb; I am the mantra, I am the clarified butter, I am the fire, I am the act of offering.
m.9.17: I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer, the grandsire; the knowable, the purifier, the syllable Om, and the Ṛk, Sāma and Yajus too.
m.9.18: I am the goal, the supporter, the Lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend; the origin, the dissolution, the ground, the treasure-house, the imperishable seed.
m.9.19: I give heat; I withhold and send forth the rain. I am immortality and also death, being and non-being, O Arjuna.
m.9.20: Knowers of the three Vedas, drinkers of soma, cleansed of sin, having worshipped me through sacrifices, pray for the way to heaven. Reaching the holy world of the lord of the gods, they enjoy in heaven the divine pleasures of the gods.
m.9.21: Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world, when their merit is exhausted they enter the world of mortals. Thus, following the dharma of the three Vedas, desiring desires, they obtain going and coming.
m.9.22: Those people who, with no other thought, meditating on me, worship me fully — for them, ever devoted, I carry the burden of gaining and preserving.
m.9.23: Even those devotees who worship other deities, endowed with faith, they too worship me alone, O son of Kuntī, though not according to the proper rule.
m.9.24: For I am the enjoyer and also the lord of all sacrifices; but they do not know me in truth, and therefore they fall.
m.9.25: Those devoted to the gods go to the gods; those devoted to the ancestors go to the ancestors; worshippers of spirits go to the spirits; and those who worship me come to me.
m.9.26: Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water — that devotional offering of the pure-minded one I accept lit. eat.
m.9.27: Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, whatever austerity you perform, O son of Kuntī — do that as an offering to me.
m.9.28: Thus you will be freed from the bonds of action, which bear good and evil fruits; with your self joined in the yoga of renunciation, liberated, you will come to me.
m.9.29: I am the same towards all beings; none is hateful to me, none dear. But those who worship me with devotion are in me, and I too am in them.
m.9.30: Even if one of very evil conduct worships me with undivided devotion, he should be regarded as righteous, for he has rightly resolved.
m.9.31: Quickly he becomes righteous of soul and attains lasting peace. O son of Kuntī, know for certain: My devotee never perishes.
m.9.32: For, O Pārtha, those who take refuge in me, even those who may be of sinful birth, and women, vaiśyas and śūdras too, reach the supreme goal.
m.9.33: How much more then holy brāhmaṇas and devoted royal sages! Having come to this transient, joyless world, worship me.
m.9.34: Fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, sacrifice to me, bow down to me. Having thus disciplined yourself, with me as your supreme goal, you will come to me alone.
m.9.iti: Oṃ Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the ninth adhyāya, named Rājavidyārājaguhyayoga, the yoga of the sovereign knowledge and the sovereign secret.
m.10.1: The Lord said: Again, O mighty-armed one, hear my supreme word, which I shall speak to you, who take delight in it, out of a wish for your welfare.
m.10.2: Neither the hosts of gods nor the great sages know my origin, for I am in every way the source of the gods and of the great sages.
m.10.3: He who knows me as unborn and beginningless, the great Lord of the worlds — he, undeluded among mortals, is freed from all sins.
m.10.4: Understanding, knowledge, freedom from delusion, forbearance, truthfulness, self-restraint, tranquillity, pleasure, pain, coming into being, ceasing to be, fear and also fearlessness,
m.10.5: non-violence, equanimity, contentment, austerity, giving, fame and infamy — these diverse states of beings arise from me alone.
m.10.6: The seven great sages, the four ancient ones, and likewise the Manus — sharing my nature, they were born from my mind; from them have come these creatures in the world.
m.10.7: He who truly knows this manifest glory and power of mine is united with me through unwavering yoga; of this there is no doubt.
m.10.8: I am the origin of all; from me everything proceeds. Understanding this, the wise worship me, filled with devotion.
m.10.9: With their minds on me, their lives given to me, enlightening one another and always speaking of me, they are content and they rejoice.
m.10.10: To them, ever united with me and worshipping with love, I give that yoga of understanding by which they come to me.
m.10.11: Out of compassion for them alone, I, dwelling within their own being, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge.
m.10.12: Arjuna said: You are the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the supreme purifier; the eternal divine Person, the primal God, unborn, all-pervading —
m.10.13: so all the sages declare you, and likewise the divine sage Nārada, Asita, Devala and Vyāsa; and you yourself tell me so.
m.10.14: All this that you tell me, O Keśava, I consider true; for neither the gods nor the demons know your manifestation, O Lord.
m.10.15: You alone know yourself by yourself, O Supreme Person, O source of beings, O lord of beings, O God of gods, O lord of the world.
m.10.16: You should describe, without leaving anything out, your own divine glories, by which glories you pervade these worlds and abide in them.
m.10.17: How may I know you, O Yogin, by constantly meditating on you? And in what various aspects are you to be contemplated by me, O Lord?
m.10.18: Tell again in detail of your yoga-power and glory, O Janārdana; for I am not satiated hearing this nectar.
m.10.19: The Lord said: Very well, I shall tell you of my divine glories — the principal ones, O best of the Kurus; for there is no end to my extent.
m.10.20: I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, that dwells in the heart of every being; I am also the beginning, the middle and the end of beings.
m.10.21: Among the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu; among lights, the radiant sun; I am Marīci among the Maruts; among the stars I am the moon.
m.10.22: Among the Vedas I am the Sāmaveda; among the gods I am Vāsava (Indra); among the senses I am the mind; in beings I am consciousness.
m.10.23: Among the Rudras I am Śaṅkara; among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, the lord of wealth Kubera; among the Vasus I am fire; among the peaks I am Meru.
m.10.24: And among household priests, O Pārtha, know me to be the chief, Bṛhaspati; among commanders of armies I am Skanda; among bodies of water I am the ocean.
m.10.25: Among the great sages I am Bhṛgu; among utterances I am the one syllable Oṃ; among sacrifices I am the sacrifice of japa; among immovable things, the Himālaya.
m.10.26: Among all trees I am the Aśvattha sacred fig, and among the divine sages Nārada; among the Gandharvas I am Citraratha, and among the perfected ones the sage Kapila.
m.10.27: Among horses know me to be Uccaiḥśravas, born of the nectar from the churning of the ocean; among lordly elephants Airāvata, and among men the king.
m.10.28: Among weapons I am the thunderbolt; among cows I am Kāmadhuk the wish-fulfilling cow; I am Kandarpa, the cause of procreation; among serpents I am Vāsuki.
m.10.29: Among the Nāgas I am Ananta; among water-dwellers I am Varuṇa; among the ancestors I am Aryaman; and among those who restrain I am Yama.
m.10.30: Among the Daityas I am Prahlāda; among reckoners I am Time; among beasts I am the lion, and among birds Vainateya (Garuḍa).
m.10.31: Among purifiers I am the wind; among wielders of weapons I am Rāma; among sea-creatures I am the makara, and among rivers I am Jāhnavī the Gaṅgā.
m.10.32: Of creations I am the beginning, the end and also the middle, O Arjuna. Of sciences I am the science of the Self; of those who debate I am the reasoned discourse.
m.10.33: Among letters I am the letter “a”, and of compounds the dvandva copulative. I alone am imperishable Time; I am the Sustainer facing in all directions.
m.10.34: I am all-seizing death, and the origin of those yet to be. Among feminine qualities I am fame, prosperity, speech, memory, intelligence, steadfastness and forbearance.
m.10.35: Likewise among the Sāman hymns I am the Bṛhat-sāman; among metres the Gāyatrī; among months I am Mārgaśīrṣa; among seasons the flower-bearing spring.
m.10.36: Of cheats I am gambling; of the splendid I am the splendour. I am victory, I am resolve; of the good I am the goodness.
m.10.37: Among the Vṛṣṇis I am Vāsudeva; among the Pāṇḍavas Dhanañjaya; among sages too I am Vyāsa; among seers the seer Uśanā.
m.10.38: Of those who subdue I am the rod of punishment; of those seeking victory I am statecraft; of secrets I am silence; of the wise I am wisdom.
m.10.39: And whatever is the seed of all beings, that I am, O Arjuna. There is no being, moving or unmoving, that could exist without me.
m.10.40: There is no end to my divine manifestations, O scorcher of foes. This extent of my glory has been declared by me only by way of illustration.
m.10.41: Whatever being is glorious, prosperous or mighty, know that to have sprung from a fraction of my splendour.
m.10.42: But what need is there for you to know all this in detail, O Arjuna? I stand, sustaining this entire universe with a single fraction of myself.
m.10.iti: Oṃ Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the tenth adhyāya, named Vibhūtiyoga, the yoga of the divine manifestations.
m.11.1: Arjuna said: Out of grace towards me, you have spoken the supreme secret word known as adhyātma (concerning the Self); by it this delusion of mine is gone.
m.11.2: For I have heard from you in detail of the origin and dissolution of beings, O lotus-eyed one, and also of your imperishable greatness.
m.11.3: It is just as you have described yourself, O Supreme Lord. Yet I wish to see your sovereign form, O Supreme Person.
m.11.4: If you think that it can be seen by me, O Lord, then, O Lord of yoga, show me your imperishable Self.
m.11.5: The Lord said: Behold, O Pārtha, my forms by the hundreds and thousands, of many kinds, divine, of many colours and shapes.
m.11.6: Behold the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and likewise the Maruts; behold many wonders never seen before, O Bhārata.
m.11.7: Behold now, O Guḍākeśa, the entire universe, moving and unmoving, standing as one here in my body, and whatever else you wish to see.
m.11.8: But you cannot see me with these very eyes of yours. I give you a divine eye; behold my sovereign yoga.
m.11.9: Sañjaya said: Having spoken thus, O King, Hari, the great Lord of yoga, then showed Pārtha his supreme sovereign form.
m.11.10: A form with many mouths and eyes, with many wondrous sights, with many divine ornaments, with many divine weapons raised,
m.11.11: wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with divine fragrances, full of every wonder, the radiant God, infinite, facing in all directions.
m.11.12: If the light of a thousand suns were to rise at once in the sky, that might resemble the splendour of that great Being.
m.11.13: There, in the body of the God of gods, the son of Pāṇḍu then saw the entire universe, divided in many ways, standing as one.
m.11.14: Then Dhanañjaya, filled with amazement, his hair standing on end, bowed his head to the God and, with joined palms, spoke.
m.11.15: Arjuna said: I see in your body, O God, all the gods and likewise the hosts of various beings; Brahmā the lord seated on the lotus, all the sages, and the divine serpents.
m.11.16: I see you with many arms, bellies, mouths and eyes, of endless form on every side; I see no end, no middle, nor again your beginning, O Lord of the universe, O universal form.
m.11.17: I see you wearing a crown, bearing a mace and a discus, a mass of radiance shining on every side, hard to behold all around, with the brilliance of blazing fire and sun, immeasurable.
m.11.18: You are the imperishable, the supreme to be known; you are the ultimate resting-place of this universe; you are the undying guardian of the eternal dharma; you are, I hold, the primeval Person.
m.11.19: I see you without beginning, middle or end, of infinite power, with countless arms, the moon and sun your eyes, your mouth a blazing fire, scorching this universe with your own radiance.
m.11.20: For this space between heaven and earth, and every direction, is pervaded by you alone. Seeing this wondrous, terrible form of yours, O great-souled one, the three worlds tremble.
m.11.21: These hosts of gods enter into you; some, afraid, praise you with joined palms. Crying “May it be well!”, hosts of great sages and perfected ones praise you with abundant hymns.
m.11.22: The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus and the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, the Maruts and the Ūṣmapas (ancestors), and the hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras and Siddhas — all gaze at you in amazement.
m.11.23: Seeing your mighty form with many mouths and eyes, O mighty-armed one, with many arms, thighs and feet, many bellies, terrible with many tusks, the worlds are terrified, and so am I.
m.11.24: Seeing you touching the sky, blazing, many-coloured, with mouths wide open and huge blazing eyes, my inmost self is shaken, and I find neither steadiness nor peace, O Viṣṇu.
m.11.25: Merely seeing your mouths, terrible with tusks and like the fire of time's end, I know not the directions and find no refuge. Be gracious, O Lord of gods, O abode of the world!
m.11.26: And all these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with the hosts of kings, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and likewise that son of a charioteer Karṇa, along with the chief warriors of our side as well,
m.11.27: are rushing into your mouths, terrible with fangs and frightful. Some are seen stuck in the gaps between the teeth, with their heads crushed to powder.
m.11.28: As the many torrents of rivers rush towards the ocean alone, so these heroes of the world of men enter your mouths, flaming all around.
m.11.29: As moths with swelling speed enter a blazing fire to their destruction, just so do the worlds too, with swelling speed, enter your mouths to their destruction.
m.11.30: Devouring all the worlds on every side with your flaming mouths, you lick your lips. Filling the whole universe with brilliance, your fierce rays scorch, O Viṣṇu.
m.11.31: Tell me who you are, of such fierce form. Salutation to you, O best of gods; be gracious. I wish to know you, the Primal One, for I do not understand your working.
m.11.32: The Lord said: I am Time, grown mighty, the destroyer of the worlds, engaged here in annihilating the worlds. Even without you, all the warriors arrayed in the opposing armies shall cease to be.
m.11.33: Therefore arise and win glory; conquering your enemies, enjoy a prosperous kingdom. They have already been slain by me alone; be merely the instrument, O Savyasācin.
m.11.34: Droṇa and Bhīṣma and Jayadratha, Karṇa and the other heroic warriors as well — already slain by me — do you slay; do not be distressed. Fight; you shall conquer your rivals in battle.
m.11.35: Sañjaya said: Having heard these words of Keśava, the diademed one Arjuna, with joined palms, trembling, bowed down and, prostrating himself, terribly afraid, spoke again to Kṛṣṇa in a faltering voice.
m.11.36: Arjuna said: Rightly, O Hṛṣīkeśa, does the world rejoice and delight in your praise; the demons flee in fear to all directions, and all the hosts of Siddhas bow down to you.
m.11.37: And why should they not bow to you, O great-souled one, who are greater even than Brahmā, the original creator? O Infinite, Lord of gods, abode of the world, you are the Imperishable — being and non-being, and that which is beyond both.
m.11.38: You are the Primal God, the ancient Person; you are the supreme resting-place of this universe. You are the knower and what is to be known, and the supreme abode. By you the universe is pervaded, O you of infinite forms.
m.11.39: You are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, the Moon, Prajāpati, and the great-grandfather. Salutations, salutations to you a thousand times, and again and yet again salutations, salutations to you!
m.11.40: Salutation to you in front and behind; salutation to you on every side, O All. Of infinite strength and immeasurable valour, you pervade everything; therefore you are all.
m.11.41: Whatever I have said rashly, thinking you a friend — “O Kṛṣṇa, O Yādava, O friend” — not knowing this greatness of yours, out of carelessness or even out of affection,
m.11.42: and whatever disrespect was shown to you in jest, while at play, in rest, sitting, or at meals, when alone or in the presence of others, O Acyuta — for that I beg forgiveness of you, the Immeasurable.
m.11.43: You are the father of this world, of all that moves and moves not; you are its object of worship and its most venerable teacher. There is none equal to you — how then could another be greater — even in the three worlds, O you of incomparable power?
m.11.44: Therefore, bowing down and prostrating my body, I seek the grace of you, the adorable Lord. As a father bears with a son, a friend with a friend, a lover with the beloved, so should you bear with me, O God.
m.11.45: Having seen what was never seen before, I am thrilled, and yet my mind is shaken with fear. Show me that very form of yours, O God; be gracious, O Lord of gods, abode of the world.
m.11.46: I wish to see you just as before, wearing a crown, bearing a mace, discus in hand. Assume that very four-armed form, O thousand-armed one, O you of universal form.
m.11.47: The Lord said: Being pleased with you, O Arjuna, I have by my own yoga-power shown you this supreme form — radiant, universal, infinite, primal — which no one other than you has seen before.
m.11.48: Not by the Vedas, sacrifices or study, not by gifts, nor by rituals, nor by severe austerities can I be seen in such a form in the world of men by anyone other than you, O great hero of the Kurus.
m.11.49: Let there be no distress for you, nor bewilderment, from seeing this terrible form of mine such as it is. Free from fear and glad at heart, behold once more that very form of mine — here it is.
m.11.50: Sañjaya said: Having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vāsudeva showed his own form once more; and the great-souled one, becoming again of gentle form, consoled him who was frightened.
m.11.51: Arjuna said: Having seen this gentle human form of yours, O Janārdana, I have now become composed in mind and have returned to my natural state.
m.11.52: The Lord said: This form of mine which you have seen is very hard to behold; even the gods are ever longing for a sight of this form.
m.11.53: Not by the Vedas, not by austerity, not by charity, nor by sacrifice can I be seen in such a form as you have seen me.
m.11.54: But by undivided devotion, O Arjuna, I can be known in this form, and seen in truth, and entered into, O scorcher of foes.
m.11.55: He who does work for me, who holds me as supreme, who is devoted to me, free from attachment, and without enmity towards any being, comes to me, O Pāṇḍava.
m.11.iti: Oṃ Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the eleventh adhyāya, named Viśvarūpadarśanayoga, the yoga of the vision of the universal form.
m.12.1: Arjuna said: Those devotees who, ever steadfast in this way, worship you, and those too who worship the Imperishable, the Unmanifest: of these, who are the better knowers of yoga?
m.12.2: The Lord said: Those who, fixing their mind on me, worship me, ever steadfast and endowed with supreme faith: they are considered by me the most perfectly established in yoga.
m.12.3: But those who worship the Imperishable, the Indefinable, the Unmanifest, the All-pervading, the Unthinkable, the Unchanging (standing like an anvil), the Immovable, the Eternal,
m.12.4: having fully restrained the group of senses, even-minded everywhere, delighting in the welfare of all beings — they too reach me alone.
m.12.5: The difficulty is greater for those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest; for the unmanifest goal is reached with hardship by embodied beings.
m.12.6: But those who, having surrendered all actions to me, holding me as the highest, worship me meditating on me with undivided yoga,
m.12.7: for them, whose minds are fixed in me, I become before long the deliverer from the ocean of death-bound worldly existence, O Pārtha.
m.12.8: Fix your mind on me alone; place your intellect in me. Thereafter you will dwell in me alone; there is no doubt.
m.12.9: If, however, you cannot fix your mind steadily on me, then seek to reach me through the yoga of practice, O Dhanañjaya.
m.12.10: If you are incapable even of practice, be intent on work for me; even performing actions for my sake, you will attain perfection.
m.12.11: If you are unable to do even this, then, taking refuge in my yoga, self-controlled, give up the fruits of all actions.
m.12.12: Knowledge is indeed better than practice; meditation excels knowledge; renunciation of the fruits of action excels meditation; from renunciation, peace follows immediately.
m.12.13: He who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from “mine” and from ego, even in sorrow and joy, forgiving,
m.12.14: ever content, a yogī, self-controlled, firm in resolve, with mind and intellect offered to me — he who is my devotee is dear to me.
m.12.15: He from whom the world does not shrink, and who does not shrink from the world, who is free from elation, impatience, fear and anxiety — he too is dear to me.
m.12.16: He who is free from expectation, pure, skilful, unconcerned, untroubled, who has renounced all undertakings — he who is my devotee is dear to me.
m.12.17: He who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor craves, who has renounced both good and evil, full of devotion — that one is dear to me.
m.12.18: Alike to foe and friend, and likewise in honour and dishonour, alike in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, free from attachment,
m.12.19: the same in blame and praise, silent, content with whatever comes, without a fixed home, steady-minded, full of devotion — that man is dear to me.
