m.12.20: But those who, full of faith, holding me as supreme, follow this immortal righteous teaching as it has been declared — those devotees are exceedingly dear to me.
m.12.iti: Oṃ Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the twelfth adhyāya, named Bhaktiyoga, the yoga of devotion.
m.13.1: Arjuna said: Prakṛti and Puruṣa, the field and the knower of the field, knowledge and that which is to be known: this I wish to know, O Keśava.
m.13.2: The Lord said: This body, O son of Kuntī, is called the field; the one who knows it, those who know these things call the knower of the field.
m.13.3: Know me also, O Bhārata, as the knower of the field in every field. The knowledge of the field and its knower — that, in my view, is knowledge.
m.13.4: What that field is, what it is like, what its modifications are, and from what it arises; and who he the knower is and what his powers are — hear that from me in brief.
m.13.5: It has been sung by the seers in many ways, separately in various Vedic hymns, and also in the well-reasoned and decisive words of the Brahma-sūtras.
m.13.6: The great elements, the ego-sense, the intellect, and the unmanifest; the ten senses and the one mind, and the five objects of the senses;
m.13.7: desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate body, awareness, and steadiness — this, in brief, is declared to be the field together with its modifications.
m.13.8: Absence of pride, absence of pretence, non-violence, forbearance, uprightness, service of the teacher, purity, steadfastness, self-restraint;
m.13.9: dispassion towards the objects of the senses, and absence of egoism; seeing the evil of pain in birth, death, old age and disease;
m.13.10: non-attachment, no clinging to son, wife, home and the like, and constant even-mindedness in the face of the desired and the undesired;
m.13.11: unswerving devotion to me through undivided yoga; resorting to solitary places, and no delight in crowds of people;
m.13.12: constancy in knowledge of the Self, and seeing the goal of knowledge of truth — this is declared to be knowledge; what is contrary to it is ignorance.
m.13.13: I shall declare that which is to be known, knowing which one attains immortality: the beginningless supreme Brahman, which is said to be neither being nor non-being.
m.13.14: With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads and faces everywhere, with ears everywhere, That abides in the world, enveloping all.
m.13.15: Shining through the functions of all the senses, yet devoid of all senses; unattached, yet sustaining all; free of the guṇas, yet the experiencer of the guṇas.
m.13.16: Outside and inside beings, unmoving and also moving; because of its subtlety That is not to be known; That is far away and also near.
m.13.17: Undivided, yet it abides in beings as if divided; That is to be known as the sustainer of beings, their devourer and their creator.
m.13.18: That is the light even of lights; it is said to lie beyond darkness. It is knowledge, the knowable, and the goal of knowledge, seated in the heart of all.
m.13.19: Thus the field, as well as knowledge and the knowable, have been told in brief. My devotee, understanding this, becomes fit for my state of being.
m.13.20: Know that Prakṛti and Puruṣa are both beginningless; and know that the modifications and the guṇas are born of Prakṛti.
m.13.21: Prakṛti is said to be the cause in the producing of effects and instruments; Puruṣa is said to be the cause in the experiencing of pleasure and pain.
m.13.22: For Puruṣa, abiding in Prakṛti, experiences the guṇas born of Prakṛti; attachment to the guṇas is the cause of its births in good and evil wombs.
m.13.23: The witness, the permitter, the sustainer, the experiencer, the great Lord, and also called the supreme Self — such is the highest Puruṣa in this body.
m.13.24: He who thus knows Puruṣa, and Prakṛti together with the guṇas, is not born again, however he may be living.
m.13.25: Some, through meditation, see the Self in the self by the self; others through the yoga of Sāṅkhya, and still others through the yoga of action.
m.13.26: But others, not knowing the Self in this way, worship having heard of it from others; they too, devoted to what they have heard, certainly cross beyond death.
m.13.27: Whatever being comes into existence, whether unmoving or moving, know that it arises from the union of the field and the knower of the field, O best of the Bharatas.
m.13.28: He who sees the supreme Lord abiding equally in all beings, the imperishable among the perishing — he truly sees.
m.13.29: For, seeing the Lord equally established everywhere, he does not harm the Self by the self; therefore he goes to the supreme goal.
m.13.30: He who sees that all actions are performed in every way by Prakṛti alone, and likewise sees the Self as not the doer — he truly sees.
m.13.31: When one perceives the separate existence of beings as resting in the One, and their expansion from That alone, then one attains Brahman.
m.13.32: Being beginningless and free from qualities, this imperishable supreme Self, though dwelling in the body, O Kaunteya, neither acts nor is tainted.
m.13.33: Just as the all-pervading space, because of its subtlety, is not tainted, so the Self, abiding everywhere in the body, is not tainted.
m.13.34: Just as the one sun illumines this whole world, so the possessor of the field illumines the whole field, O Bhārata.
m.13.35: Those who, with the eye of knowledge, thus know the difference between the field and its knower, and how beings are freed from Prakṛti, go to the Supreme.
m.13.iti: Oṃ Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the thirteenth adhyāya, named Kṣetrakṣetrajñavibhāgayoga, the yoga of the distinction between the field and its knower.
m.14.1: The Lord said: I shall again declare the supreme knowledge, the highest among all knowledges, knowing which all the sages have gone from here to the supreme perfection.
m.14.2: Having taken refuge in this knowledge, those who have come to share my nature are not born even at the creation, nor are they troubled at the dissolution.
m.14.3: The great Brahman (primal nature) is my womb; in it I place the seed. From that, O Bhārata, comes the birth of all beings.
m.14.4: Whatever forms come into being in all wombs, O Kaunteya, the great Brahman is their womb, and I am the seed-giving father.
m.14.5: Sattva, rajas and tamas — these guṇas born of prakṛti bind fast in the body, O mighty-armed one, the imperishable embodied self.
m.14.6: Of these, sattva, being stainless, is illuminating and free from ill; it binds, O sinless one, through attachment to happiness and attachment to knowledge.
m.14.7: Know rajas to be of the nature of passion, arising from craving and attachment; it binds the embodied one, O Kaunteya, through attachment to action.
m.14.8: But know tamas to be born of ignorance, deluding all embodied beings; it binds, O Bhārata, through heedlessness, sloth and sleep.
m.14.9: Sattva attaches one to happiness, rajas to action, O Bhārata; but tamas, veiling knowledge, attaches one to heedlessness.
m.14.10: Sattva prevails, O Bhārata, overpowering rajas and tamas; rajas prevails, overpowering sattva and tamas; and likewise tamas prevails, overpowering sattva and rajas.
m.14.11: When the light of knowledge arises through all the gates of this body, then one should know that sattva has increased.
m.14.12: Greed, activity, the undertaking of actions, restlessness, longing — these arise when rajas has increased, O best of the Bharatas.
m.14.13: Darkness, inertia, heedlessness and delusion — these arise when tamas has increased, O joy of the Kurus.
m.14.14: When the embodied one meets dissolution (death) while sattva is predominant, then he attains the stainless worlds of those who know the highest.
m.14.15: Meeting death in rajas, one is born among those attached to action; likewise, dying in tamas, one is born in the wombs of the deluded.
m.14.16: The fruit of good action, they say, is sāttvika and stainless; but the fruit of rajas is sorrow, and the fruit of tamas is ignorance.
m.14.17: From sattva arises knowledge, and from rajas greed; from tamas arise heedlessness and delusion, and ignorance too.
m.14.18: Those established in sattva go upward; the rājasika remain in the middle; the tāmasika, abiding in the function of the lowest guṇa, go downward.
m.14.19: When the seer beholds no agent other than the guṇas, and knows That which is beyond the guṇas, he attains my being.
m.14.20: Having transcended these three guṇas, from which the body arises, the embodied one, freed from the sorrows of birth, death and old age, attains immortality.
m.14.21: Arjuna said: By what marks is one known who has transcended these three guṇas, O Lord? What is his conduct, and how does he go beyond these three guṇas?
m.14.22: The Lord said: O Pāṇḍava, he does not hate illumination, activity, or delusion when they arise, nor does he long for them when they cease.
m.14.23: He who, sitting as if indifferent, is not shaken by the guṇas; who, knowing “the guṇas alone are acting”, stays firm and does not waver;
m.14.24: Alike in sorrow and joy, abiding in the Self, regarding a clod, a stone and gold as equal, the same towards the pleasant and the unpleasant, steadfast, equal in blame and praise of himself;
m.14.25: The same in honour and dishonour, the same towards the side of friend and foe, having renounced all undertakings — he is said to have transcended the guṇas.
m.14.26: And he who serves me with the yoga of devotion that never strays, he, having gone fully beyond these guṇas, becomes fit for becoming Brahman.
m.14.27: For I am the foundation of Brahman, of the immortal and imperishable, of the eternal dharma, and of absolute bliss.
m.14.iti: Oṃ Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the fourteenth adhyāya, named Guṇatrayavibhāgayoga, the yoga of the division of the three guṇas.
m.15.1: The Lord said: They speak of the imperishable aśvattha tree with its roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic hymns. He who knows it is a knower of the Veda.
m.15.2: Its branches spread below and above, nourished by the guṇas, with sense-objects as their shoots; and below, in the world of humans, its roots stretch out, binding beings to action.
m.15.3: Its form is not perceived here as such, nor its end, nor its beginning, nor its foundation. Having cut down this firmly rooted aśvattha with the strong axe of non-attachment —
m.15.4: — then that goal must be sought, having reached which they do not return again: “I take refuge in that primal Person alone, from whom the ancient flow of creation has streamed forth.”
m.15.5: Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, ever devoted to the Self, with desires turned away, released from the dualities known as pleasure and pain, the undeluded reach that imperishable goal.
m.15.6: Neither the sun illumines it, nor the moon, nor fire; having gone there, they do not return — that is my supreme abode.
m.15.7: An eternal portion of myself alone, having become the individual soul in the world of living beings, draws to itself the senses — the mind and the five others — which abide in prakṛti.
m.15.8: When the lord of the body acquires a body and when he departs from it, he takes these along and goes, as the wind carries scents from their source.
m.15.9: Presiding over the ear, the eye, touch, taste and smell, and the mind too, he enjoys the sense-objects.
m.15.10: The deluded do not perceive him as he departs, or stays, or enjoys, joined with the guṇas; those with the eye of knowledge see.
m.15.11: Striving yogis see him established in themselves; but the undisciplined, lacking discernment, do not see him even though they strive.
m.15.12: The radiance residing in the sun which lights up the whole world, and that which is in the moon and in fire — know that radiance to be mine.
m.15.13: Entering the earth, I sustain all beings by my energy; and becoming the sap-filled Soma, I nourish all plants.
m.15.14: Becoming the digestive fire Vaiśvānara and dwelling in the bodies of living beings, joined with prāṇa and apāna, I digest the fourfold food.
m.15.15: And I am seated in the heart of all; from me come memory and knowledge, and their loss as well. I alone am to be known through all the Vedas; I am the author of Vedānta and the knower of the Vedas.
m.15.16: There are two persons in the world, the perishable and the imperishable. All beings are the perishable; the unchanging one is called the imperishable.
m.15.17: But the highest Person is another, called the Supreme Self, who, as the imperishable Lord, pervades the three worlds and sustains them.
m.15.18: Since I transcend the perishable and am higher even than the imperishable, therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as Puruṣottama, the Supreme Person.
m.15.19: He who, undeluded, thus knows me as the Supreme Person, he, knowing all, worships me with his whole being, O Bhārata.
m.15.20: Thus this most secret teaching has been spoken by me, O sinless one. Understanding this, one becomes wise and one's duties are fulfilled, O Bhārata.
m.15.iti: Oṃ Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the fifteenth adhyāya, named Puruṣottamayoga, the yoga of the Supreme Person.
m.16.1: The Lord said: The Blessed Lord said: Fearlessness, purity of mind, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, charity, self-restraint and sacrifice, study of the scriptures, austerity, uprightness,
m.16.2: non-violence, truthfulness, absence of anger, renunciation, tranquillity, absence of slander, compassion towards beings, freedom from greed, gentleness, modesty, absence of fickleness,
m.16.3: vigour, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, absence of malice, absence of excessive pride — these belong to one born to the divine endowment, O Bhārata.
m.16.4: Hypocrisy, arrogance and conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance — these belong to one born to the demonic endowment, O Pārtha.
m.16.5: The divine endowment is deemed to lead to liberation, the demonic to bondage. Do not grieve, O Pāṇḍava; you are born to the divine endowment.
m.16.6: There are two kinds of created beings in this world: the divine and the demonic. The divine has been described at length; now, O Pārtha, hear from me about the demonic.
m.16.7: Demonic people know neither right action nor right abstention. Neither purity, nor good conduct, nor truth is found in them.
m.16.8: They say the world is without truth, without foundation, without a Lord, not produced by any orderly sequence — what else is its cause but desire?
m.16.9: Holding to this view, these lost souls of little understanding, of cruel deeds, rise up as enemies of the world for its destruction.
m.16.10: Resorting to insatiable desire, filled with hypocrisy, pride and arrogance, having seized wrong notions through delusion, they act with impure vows.
m.16.11: Clinging to immeasurable anxiety that ends only with death, holding the enjoyment of desires as the highest aim, convinced that this is all,
m.16.12: bound by hundreds of nooses of hope, given over to desire and anger, they strive to amass wealth by unjust means for the enjoyment of desires.
m.16.13: “This I have gained today; this desire I shall fulfil; this is mine, and this wealth too shall be mine hereafter.”
m.16.14: “That enemy has been slain by me, and I shall slay others too. I am the master, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, mighty and happy.”
m.16.15: “I am wealthy and of noble birth; who else is equal to me? I shall sacrifice, I shall give, I shall rejoice” — thus deluded by ignorance,
m.16.16: bewildered by many thoughts, enveloped in the net of delusion, attached to the enjoyment of desires, they fall into a foul hell.
m.16.17: Self-conceited, obstinate, full of pride and the intoxication of wealth, they offer sacrifices in name only, with hypocrisy, disregarding the prescribed rules.
m.16.18: Given over to egoism, force, arrogance, desire and anger, these envious ones hate me, dwelling in their own bodies and in those of others.
m.16.19: Those hateful, cruel, inauspicious lowest of men I hurl again and again in the cycles of rebirth into demonic wombs alone.
m.16.20: Having entered demonic wombs, deluded birth after birth, never reaching me, O Kaunteya, they then go to the lowest state.
m.16.21: Threefold is this gate of hell, destructive of the self: desire, anger and greed. Therefore one should abandon these three.
m.16.22: A person freed from these three gates of darkness, O Kaunteya, practises what is good for the self, and thereby attains the supreme goal.
m.16.23: One who casts aside the injunctions of scripture and acts according to the impulse of desire attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal.
m.16.24: Therefore scripture is your authority in determining what should and should not be done. Knowing what is declared by scriptural injunction, you should perform action here.
m.16.iti: Oṃ Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the sixteenth adhyāya, named Daivāsurasampadvibhāgayoga, the yoga of the division between the divine and the demonic endowments.
m.17.1: Arjuna said: Those who, setting aside the injunctions of scripture, worship endowed with faith — what is their standing, O Kṛṣṇa? Is it sattva, or rajas, or tamas?
m.17.2: The Lord said: The faith of embodied beings is of three kinds, born of their own nature — sattvic, rajasic and tamasic. Hear of it.
m.17.3: The faith of everyone accords with his inner nature, O Bhārata. A person is made of faith; whatever his faith is, that indeed he is.
m.17.4: Sattvic people worship the gods; rajasic people worship yakṣas and rākṣasas; the others, tamasic people, worship departed spirits and hosts of ghosts.
m.17.5: Those people who practise fierce austerity not enjoined by scripture, joined with hypocrisy and egoism, possessed by the force of desire and attachment,
m.17.6: senseless, tormenting the aggregate of elements in the body, and me too who dwell within the body — know them to be of demonic resolve.
m.17.7: Even the food dear to each is of three kinds; so too sacrifice, austerity and giving. Hear this distinction among them.
m.17.8: Foods that increase life, vitality, strength, health, happiness and satisfaction, that are savoury, rich, sustaining and agreeable, are dear to the sattvic.
m.17.9: Foods that are bitter, sour, salty, overly hot, pungent, dry and burning are liked by the rajasic; they bring pain, grief and disease.
m.17.10: Food that is stale, tasteless, putrid and left overnight, and that which is leftover and impure, is dear to the tamasic.
m.17.11: The sacrifice that is offered as enjoined by ordinance by those who do not crave its fruit, with the mind fixed on the thought “it ought simply to be offered” — that is sattvic.
m.17.12: But that which is offered aiming at the fruit, and also for the sake of display, O best of the Bhāratas — know that sacrifice to be rajasic.
m.17.13: A sacrifice without ordinance, in which no food is distributed, without mantras, without fees to the priests, and devoid of faith, they call tamasic.
m.17.14: Worship of the gods, the twice-born, teachers and the wise; purity, straightforwardness, continence and non-violence — this is called austerity of the body.
m.17.15: Speech that causes no agitation, that is true, pleasant and beneficial, and also the practice of scriptural recitation — this is called austerity of speech.
m.17.16: Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint and purity of disposition — this is called austerity of the mind.
m.17.17: This threefold austerity, practised with supreme faith by steadfast men who do not crave the fruit, they call sattvic.
m.17.18: Austerity that is performed for the sake of respect, honour and reverence, and with hypocrisy, is declared here to be rajasic, unsteady and impermanent.
m.17.19: Austerity performed out of deluded obstinacy, with torment of oneself, or for the purpose of ruining another, is said to be tamasic.
m.17.20: A gift given with the thought “it ought to be given”, to one who does no service in return, at the proper place and time and to a worthy recipient — that gift is held to be sattvic.
m.17.21: But a gift given for the sake of a return favour, or again with a view to its fruit, and given grudgingly — that gift is held to be rajasic.
m.17.22: A gift given at the wrong place and time, to unworthy persons, without respect and with contempt — that is said to be tamasic.
m.17.23: “Om Tat Sat” — this is held to be the threefold designation of Brahman. By it were ordained of old the brāhmaṇas, the Vedas and the sacrifices.
m.17.24: Therefore, uttering “Om”, the acts of sacrifice, giving and austerity enjoined by ordinance are always begun by the expounders of Brahman.
m.17.25: Uttering “Tat”, without aiming at the fruit, the various acts of sacrifice and austerity and the acts of giving are performed by those who seek liberation.
m.17.26: The word “sat” is used in the sense of reality and in the sense of goodness; likewise, O Pārtha, the word “sat” is applied to a praiseworthy action.
m.17.27: Steadfastness in sacrifice, austerity and giving is also called “sat”; and any action done for that purpose is likewise designated “sat”.
m.17.28: Whatever is offered in oblation, given, or performed as austerity, or any act done without faith, is called “asat”, O Pārtha; it is of no avail either hereafter or here.
m.17.iti: Oṃ Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the seventeenth adhyāya, named Śraddhātrayavibhāgayoga, the yoga of the threefold division of faith.
m.18.1: Arjuna said: O mighty-armed one, I wish to know the truth of renunciation (saṃnyāsa), O Hṛṣīkeśa, and of relinquishment (tyāga), each separately, O slayer of Keśin.
m.18.2: The Lord said: The wise understand renunciation (saṃnyāsa) as the giving up of actions prompted by desire; the discerning call relinquishment (tyāga) the abandoning of the fruits of all actions.
m.18.3: Some thinkers say that action should be given up as being full of fault; others say that acts of sacrifice, giving and austerity should not be given up.
m.18.4: Hear from me the conclusion on that matter of relinquishment, O best of the Bharatas; for relinquishment, O tiger among men, is declared to be of three kinds.
m.18.5: Acts of sacrifice, giving and austerity are not to be abandoned; they must indeed be performed. Sacrifice, giving and austerity are purifiers of the wise.
m.18.6: But even these actions should be performed giving up attachment and desire for fruits; this, O Pārtha, is my settled and highest view.
m.18.7: But renunciation of prescribed action is not proper; its abandonment out of delusion is declared to be tāmasa.
m.18.8: Whoever gives up an action merely because it is painful, from fear of bodily hardship, having made such a rājasa relinquishment, does not gain the fruit of relinquishment.
m.18.9: When prescribed action is performed simply because it ought to be done, O Arjuna, giving up attachment and also the fruit, that relinquishment is considered sāttvika.
m.18.10: The relinquisher, pervaded by sattva, intelligent, his doubts cut away, neither hates disagreeable action nor clings to agreeable action.
m.18.11: For it is not possible for an embodied being to give up actions entirely; but he who relinquishes the fruit of action is called a relinquisher.
m.18.12: The threefold fruit of action — undesired, desired and mixed — comes after death to those who have not relinquished, but never to renouncers.
m.18.13: O mighty-armed one, learn from me these five causes for the accomplishment of all actions, as declared in the Sāṅkhya doctrine, which brings action to its end.
m.18.14: The seat the body, likewise the doer, the various instruments, the many distinct activities, and the divine factor as the fifth here.
m.18.15: Whatever action a man undertakes with body, speech and mind, whether right or contrary, these five are its causes.
m.18.16: This being so, he who, owing to an untrained understanding, sees the Self alone as the doer — that dull-minded one does not see.
m.18.17: He whose state is free from the sense of “I am the doer”, whose understanding is not tainted — even if he slays these worlds, he does not slay, nor is he bound.
m.18.18: Knowledge, the object of knowledge and the knower are the threefold impulse to action; the instrument, the action and the doer are the threefold composition of action.
m.18.19: Knowledge, action and the doer are declared in the enumeration of the guṇas to be of three kinds only, according to the difference of guṇas; hear of these too as they are.
m.18.20: That knowledge by which one sees in all beings one imperishable reality, undivided among the divided — know that knowledge to be sāttvika.
m.18.21: But that knowledge which, through separateness, perceives in all beings manifold entities of distinct kinds — know that knowledge to be rājasa.
m.18.22: But that which clings to a single effect as if it were the whole, without reason, not grasping the true meaning, and petty — that is declared tāmasa.
m.18.23: Action that is prescribed, free from attachment, done without attraction or aversion by one who does not crave its fruit — that is called sāttvika.
m.18.24: But action done by one who craves desires, or again by one full of ego, with great strain — that is declared rājasa.
m.18.25: Action undertaken out of delusion, without regard to consequence, loss, harm to others and one's own capacity — that is called tāmasa.
m.18.26: A doer who is free from attachment, does not speak with ego, is endowed with steadiness and zeal, and is unchanged in success and failure is called sāttvika.
m.18.27: A doer who is passionate, eager for the fruits of action, greedy, violent by nature, impure, and swayed by joy and sorrow is declared rājasa.
m.18.28: A doer who is undisciplined, vulgar, obstinate, deceitful, malicious, lazy, despondent and procrastinating is called tāmasa.
m.18.29: Hear now, O Dhanañjaya, the threefold distinction of intellect and of steadiness according to the guṇas, being told fully and one by one.
m.18.30: The intellect which knows engagement and withdrawal, what is to be done and what is not, fear and fearlessness, bondage and liberation — that intellect, O Pārtha, is sāttvika.
m.18.31: The intellect by which one understands wrongly dharma and adharma, what is to be done and what is not to be done — that intellect, O Pārtha, is rājasa.
m.18.32: The intellect which, covered by darkness, regards adharma as dharma and sees all things in reverse — that intellect, O Pārtha, is tāmasa.
m.18.33: The unwavering steadiness by which, through yoga, one holds in check the functions of the mind, the life-breath and the senses — that steadiness, O Pārtha, is sāttvika.
m.18.34: But the steadiness by which, O Arjuna, one holds to dharma, pleasure and wealth, desiring their fruits out of attachment — that steadiness, O Pārtha, is rājasa.
m.18.35: The steadiness by which a dull-witted person does not give up sleep, fear, grief, despondency and arrogance — that steadiness, O Pārtha, is tāmasa.
m.18.36: And now hear from me, O best of the Bharatas, the threefold happiness — that in which one comes to delight through practice and reaches the end of sorrow.
m.18.37: That which is like poison at first but like nectar in the end, born of the clarity of one's own intellect — that happiness is declared sāttvika.
m.18.38: That which arises from the contact of the senses with their objects, like nectar at first but like poison in the end — that happiness is held to be rājasa.
m.18.39: The happiness which deludes the self at first and in its consequence as well, arising from sleep, sloth and negligence — that is declared tāmasa.
m.18.40: There is no being, on earth or again in heaven among the gods, that could be free from these three guṇas born of prakṛti.
m.18.41: O scorcher of foes, the duties of brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas and vaiśyas, and those of śūdras, are divided by the guṇas that arise from their own nature.
m.18.42: Calmness, self-restraint, austerity, purity, forbearance and uprightness, knowledge, realisation and faith — these are the duties of a brāhmaṇa, born of his nature.
m.18.43: Valour, vigour, steadiness, skill, not fleeing in battle, generosity and lordliness — these are the duties of a kṣatriya, born of his nature.
m.18.44: Agriculture, cattle-keeping and trade are the duties of a vaiśya, born of his nature; and the duty of a śūdra, consisting of service, is likewise born of his nature.
m.18.45: Devoted each to his own duty, a person attains perfection. Hear how one devoted to his own duty finds perfection.
m.18.46: By worshipping, through his own duty, him from whom all beings arise and by whom all this is pervaded, a person attains perfection.
m.18.47: Better is one's own dharma, though imperfect, than another's dharma well performed. Doing the duty prescribed by one's own nature, one incurs no sin.
m.18.48: O son of Kuntī, one should not abandon the duty one is born to, even if it has faults; for all undertakings are covered by fault, as fire is by smoke.
m.18.49: One whose intellect is unattached everywhere, who has mastered himself and is free from cravings, attains through renunciation the supreme perfection of freedom from action.
m.18.50: Learn from me briefly, O son of Kuntī, how one who has attained perfection attains Brahman, which is the supreme culmination of knowledge.
m.18.51: Endowed with a purified intellect, restraining the self with firmness, giving up sound and the other objects of the senses, and casting aside attachment and aversion,
m.18.52: resorting to solitude, eating lightly, with speech, body and mind controlled, ever intent on the yoga of meditation, taking refuge in dispassion,
m.18.53: having given up egoism, force, arrogance, desire, anger and possessiveness, free from the sense of “mine”, and at peace — he becomes fit for becoming one with Brahman.
m.18.54: Having become Brahman, serene in spirit, he neither grieves nor desires; equal towards all beings, he attains supreme devotion to me.
m.18.55: Through devotion he truly comes to know me — how great I am and who I am in essence; then, having known me in essence, he enters into me forthwith.
m.18.56: Even while always performing all actions, one who takes refuge in me attains, by my grace, the eternal, imperishable abode.
m.18.57: Mentally renouncing all actions in me, holding me as supreme, resorting to the yoga of understanding, be always with your mind fixed on me.
m.18.58: With your mind on me, by my grace you will cross over all difficulties; but if out of egoism you will not listen, you will perish.
m.18.59: If, resorting to egoism, you think “I will not fight”, this resolve of yours is vain; your nature will compel you.
m.18.60: Bound by your own action born of your nature, O son of Kuntī, what in your delusion you do not want to do, you will do even against your will.
m.18.61: The Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, O Arjuna, causing all beings to revolve by his māyā, as if mounted on a machine.
m.18.62: Go to him alone for refuge with all your being, O Bhārata; by his grace you will attain supreme peace and the eternal abode.
m.18.63: Thus has knowledge more secret than all secrets been declared to you by me. Reflecting on it fully, do as you wish.
m.18.64: Hear again my supreme word, the most secret of all. You are dearly loved by me; therefore I shall speak what is for your good.
m.18.65: Fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, worship me, bow down to me. You will come to me alone; I promise you truly, for you are dear to me.
m.18.66: Abandoning all dharmas, come to me alone for refuge. I shall free you from all sins; do not grieve.
m.18.67: This should never be spoken by you to one without austerity, nor to one without devotion, nor to one unwilling to listen, nor to one who finds fault with me.
m.18.68: He who, having shown supreme devotion to me, will declare this supreme secret to my devotees, shall come to me alone, without doubt.
m.18.69: Among men there is none who does me dearer service than he, nor shall there be another on earth dearer to me than he.
m.18.70: And he who will study this sacred dialogue between us worships me by the sacrifice of knowledge — such is my view.
m.18.71: And the man who merely listens to it with faith and without cavilling, he too, liberated, would attain the auspicious worlds of those of meritorious deeds.
m.18.72: Has this been heard by you, O Pārtha, with a one-pointed mind? Has your delusion born of ignorance been destroyed, O Dhanañjaya?
m.18.73: Arjuna said: Delusion is destroyed, and remembrance of my true self has been regained by me through your grace, O Acyuta. I stand firm, my doubts gone; I shall do your bidding.
m.18.74: Sañjaya said: Thus I heard this wondrous, hair-raising dialogue between Vāsudeva and the great-souled Pārtha.
m.18.75: By the grace of Vyāsa I heard this supreme secret, this yoga, directly from Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of yoga, himself declaring it.
m.18.76: O King, recalling again and again this wondrous and holy dialogue between Keśava and Arjuna, I rejoice over and over.
m.18.77: And recalling again and again that most wondrous form of Hari, great is my amazement, O King, and I rejoice again and again.
m.18.78: Wherever there is Kṛṣṇa, the lord of yoga, and wherever there is Pārtha, the bearer of the bow, there are fortune, victory, prosperity and steadfast righteous conduct — such is my conviction.
m.18.iti: Oṃ Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the eighteenth adhyāya, named Mokṣasaṃnyāsayoga, the yoga of liberation through renunciation.
